exam.rules: The Life in the UK Test is a computer-based test taken at an approved test centre by most people applying for settlement (indefinite leave to remain) or British citizenship. It has 24 questions about British values, history, traditions and everyday life, all based on the official handbook 'Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents'. You have 45 minutes and need at least 18 correct answers (75%) to pass. Questions can be single-answer, true/false or 'select two'. The test costs £50 and must be booked online at least 3 days ahead; you need to bring the same ID used to book. People under 18, aged 65 or over, or with a long-term physical or mental condition (with evidence) do not need to take it, and you only need to pass once.

topics.title: Values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
options: Rule by a single political party
Compulsory attendance at a place of worship
questions.explain: The handbook lists democracy as one of the fundamental principles of British life.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which principle of British life means that everyone must follow the law?
options: Obedience to employers in all matters
questions.explain: The rule of law means everyone, including those in power, must follow the law.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which principle of British life protects people's right to make their own choices within the law?
questions.explain: Individual liberty is one of the fundamental principles listed in the handbook.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a fundamental principle of British life?
options: Support for one official religion only
Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs
Keeping religious beliefs secret by law
questions.explain: Tolerance of people with different faiths and beliefs is a fundamental principle.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is a fundamental principle of British life?
questions.explain: Taking part in community life is one of the principles listed in the handbook.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility that people living in the UK are expected to accept?
options: To respect and obey the law
To attend a place of worship
To serve in the armed forces
questions.explain: Everyone living in the UK is expected to respect and obey the law.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility expected of everyone living in the UK?
options: To agree with the government on all issues
To respect the rights of others, including their right to their own opinions
To support the same football team as their neighbours
To share their religious beliefs with others
questions.explain: Respecting the rights and opinions of others is one of the listed responsibilities.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility that comes with living in the UK?
options: To vote for the party in government
To live in the same area for life
questions.explain: Treating others fairly is listed among the responsibilities of residents.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these responsibilities should everyone in the UK accept?
options: To look after themselves and their family
To become a member of a local council
questions.explain: Looking after yourself and your family is one of the listed responsibilities.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: What responsibility do UK residents have towards their neighbourhood?
options: To look after the area in which they live and the environment
To take part in national sports events
questions.explain: Residents are expected to look after their local area and the environment.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is a freedom that the UK offers to everyone living here?
options: Freedom to ignore laws you disagree with
Freedom to carry a weapon for self-defence
questions.explain: Freedom of belief and religion is one of the freedoms listed in the handbook.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is a freedom offered to everyone in the UK?
options: Freedom to drive without a licence
Freedom from all military obligations in wartime
Freedom to choose which laws apply to you
questions.explain: Freedom of speech is one of the freedoms set out in the handbook.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is a freedom that everyone living in the UK has?
options: Freedom to refuse to pay income tax
Freedom to build anywhere without permission
Freedom from jury service in all cases
questions.explain: Freedom from unfair discrimination is one of the listed freedoms.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these rights does everyone living in the UK have?
options: The right to a free house
The right to choose their own judge
The right to avoid all police questioning
The right to a fair trial
questions.explain: Everyone in the UK has the right to a fair trial.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is a right offered by the UK?
options: The right to appoint government ministers
The right to a guaranteed job
The right to join in the election of a government
The right to veto new laws
questions.explain: Taking part in electing a government is one of the rights listed in the handbook.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: What do new citizens promise in the citizenship pledge?
options: To live in the UK for at least ten years
To join the armed forces if asked
To give their loyalty to the UK and uphold its democratic values
questions.explain: The pledge includes giving loyalty to the UK, respecting its rights and freedoms, upholding democratic values and observing its laws.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: At a citizenship ceremony, what do new citizens make in addition to an oath or affirmation of allegiance?
options: A speech about their home country
questions.explain: New citizens take an oath (or affirmation) of allegiance and then make a pledge.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: What can a person who prefers not to swear by God say at a citizenship ceremony instead of the oath?
questions.explain: People can choose a non-religious affirmation instead of the religious oath of allegiance.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: In the oath of allegiance, new citizens promise to be faithful to whom?
options: The monarch, their heirs and successors
The Speaker of the House of Commons
questions.explain: The oath is one of allegiance to the reigning monarch (King Charles III as of October 2026), his heirs and successors.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: What does the citizenship pledge commit new citizens to do with UK law?
options: Change any laws they disagree with
Follow only laws from their country of birth
questions.explain: The pledge includes a promise to observe the UK's laws faithfully.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: To apply for British citizenship or settlement, what must most applicants show besides passing the Life in the UK test?
options: They own property in the UK
They can speak and understand English to the required level
They have a UK university degree
They have a job in the public sector
questions.explain: Applicants usually need to pass the Life in the UK test and meet the English language requirement.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which publication is the Life in the UK test based on?
options: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents
questions.explain: The test questions are based on the official handbook 'Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents'.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which statement about British values is correct?
options: There is no place in British society for extremism or intolerance
Extremist views are encouraged in public debate
Intolerance is acceptable if it is within your own community
Values only apply to British-born citizens
questions.explain: The handbook states that extremism and intolerance have no place in British society.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which statement is correct about the rights and responsibilities of people who live in the UK?
options: Only citizens born in the UK have responsibilities
Rights such as free speech come with responsibilities such as obeying the law
Responsibilities apply only to people who vote
Rights can be used to break the law if necessary
questions.explain: The handbook pairs the freedoms of UK life with responsibilities that everyone is expected to accept.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the fundamental principles of British life listed in the handbook?
questions.explain: The listed principles are democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance and participation in community life.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch1 The values and principles of the UK

questions.q: Which countries make up the United Kingdom?
options: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland
England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man
questions.explain: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which countries make up 'Great Britain'?
options: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
questions.explain: Great Britain refers to England, Scotland and Wales; Northern Ireland is part of the UK but not of Great Britain.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: What is the official name of the country?
options: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
The United Kingdom of England and Scotland
questions.explain: The country's official name is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: What is the status of the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man?
options: They are Crown dependencies, not part of the UK, with their own governments
They are British overseas territories in the Caribbean
They are part of the Republic of Ireland
questions.explain: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are closely linked to the UK but are Crown dependencies with their own governments.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which of these is a British overseas territory?
questions.explain: The Falkland Islands and St Helena are examples of British overseas territories; the Isle of Man and Jersey are Crown dependencies.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which of these places is a British overseas territory rather than a Crown dependency?
questions.explain: St Helena is a British overseas territory, linked to the UK but not part of it.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Where does the UK Parliament sit?
questions.explain: The UK is governed by the Parliament sitting in Westminster.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which parts of the UK have their own devolved parliament or assembly?
questions.explain: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have parliaments or assemblies with devolved powers.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which of these is NOT part of the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The Republic of Ireland is a separate, independent country.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Is the Isle of Man part of the United Kingdom?
options: Yes, it is part of England
No, it is a Crown dependency with its own government
Yes, it is part of Scotland
No, it is part of the Republic of Ireland
questions.explain: The Isle of Man is a Crown dependency, not part of the UK.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Northern Ireland is located on which island?
questions.explain: Northern Ireland is in the north-east of the island of Ireland and is part of the UK.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which statement about the British overseas territories is correct?
options: They have a close link with the UK but are not part of it
They are represented by their own MPs at Westminster
questions.explain: Overseas territories such as the Falklands are linked to the UK but are not part of it.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which statement about the Channel Islands is correct?
options: They are governed directly by the Scottish Parliament
They elect MPs to the House of Commons
questions.explain: The Channel Islands are Crown dependencies with their own governments.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which country is part of the UK but not part of Great Britain?
questions.explain: Great Britain is England, Scotland and Wales; Northern Ireland is the fourth country of the UK.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: Which statement about the UK is correct?
options: Each country of the UK is fully independent
England has its own separate parliament apart from Westminster
Only England is governed by the UK Parliament
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved administrations, but the UK Parliament covers the whole UK
questions.explain: Devolved bodies handle some matters in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, while the UK Parliament at Westminster governs the UK as a whole.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch2 What is the UK?

questions.q: How did the first people reach Britain during the Stone Age?
options: They walked across a land bridge that joined Britain to the continent
They came by boat from Iceland
questions.explain: Early hunter-gatherers crossed on foot when Britain was still connected to the continent by land.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: Roughly when did Britain become permanently separated from the continent by the Channel?
questions.explain: Britain was finally cut off from the continent around 10,000 years ago.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: About how long ago did the first farmers arrive in Britain?
questions.explain: The first farmers came to Britain roughly 6,000 years ago, probably from south-east Europe.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: In which English county is Stonehenge?
questions.explain: Stonehenge, a prehistoric monument, stands in Wiltshire.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: Where is Skara Brae, the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe?
options: Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland
questions.explain: Skara Brae on Orkney is the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: During which period did people in Britain learn to make bronze and bury their dead in round barrows?
questions.explain: The Bronze Age began about 4,000 years ago; people were often buried in round barrows.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: Maiden Castle is an impressive example of what kind of Iron Age site?
questions.explain: Maiden Castle in Dorset is a large Iron Age hill fort.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: In which county is the Iron Age hill fort Maiden Castle?
questions.explain: Maiden Castle is in Dorset.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: What language did people in Britain speak during the Iron Age?
questions.explain: Iron Age people spoke a language belonging to the Celtic family.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: When were the first coins minted in Britain?
questions.explain: The first coins made in Britain date from the Iron Age; some carried the names of Iron Age kings.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: Early Britain

questions.q: Who led an unsuccessful Roman invasion of Britain in 55 BC?
questions.explain: Julius Caesar's attempted invasion in 55 BC did not succeed.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: In what year did the Roman Emperor Claudius lead a successful invasion of Britain?
questions.explain: The Romans under Claudius invaded in AD 43 and went on to occupy much of Britain.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: Which tribal queen fought against the Romans and has a statue near Westminster Bridge?
questions.explain: Boudicca, queen of the Iceni in what is now eastern England, led resistance to the Romans.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: Boudicca was queen of which tribe?
questions.explain: Boudicca led the Iceni of eastern England against Roman rule.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: Why was Hadrian's Wall built?
options: To defend London from the Vikings
To mark the border with Wales
To keep out the Picts in the north
questions.explain: Emperor Hadrian built the wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts, ancestors of the Scottish people.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: Which of these are well-known forts along Hadrian's Wall?
questions.explain: Housesteads and Vindolanda are popular parts of Hadrian's Wall, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: For roughly how long did the Romans stay in Britain?
questions.explain: The Romans remained for around 400 years, leaving in AD 410.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: In what year did the Romans leave Britain?
questions.explain: Roman armies left Britain in AD 410 to defend other parts of the empire.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: Which of these did the Romans bring to Britain?
options: Roads, public buildings and a structure of law
questions.explain: The Romans built roads and public buildings, created a legal structure and introduced new plants and animals.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: Which part of Britain did the Romans never fully conquer?
options: Most of what is now Scotland
questions.explain: The Romans did not conquer all of Scotland; Hadrian's Wall marked the northern limit for long periods.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Romans

questions.q: Which peoples invaded Britain after the Romans left?
questions.explain: After AD 410, tribes from northern Europe – the Jutes, Angles and Saxons – invaded Britain.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Anglo-Saxons

questions.q: By about what year had Anglo-Saxon kingdoms been established in Britain?
questions.explain: By around AD 600 Anglo-Saxon kingdoms covered much of what is now England.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Anglo-Saxons

questions.q: Where is the burial place of an Anglo-Saxon king, Sutton Hoo?
questions.explain: Sutton Hoo in Suffolk is the burial site of an Anglo-Saxon king, probably of East Anglia, buried with treasure and armour in a ship.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Anglo-Saxons

questions.q: Which parts of Britain largely remained free of Anglo-Saxon rule?
questions.explain: Wales and much of Scotland stayed largely free from Anglo-Saxon rule.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Anglo-Saxons

questions.q: Who was the first Archbishop of Canterbury?
questions.explain: St Augustine led missionaries from Rome to southern England and became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Anglo-Saxons

questions.q: Which missionary founded a monastery on the island of Iona?
questions.explain: St Columba founded a monastery on Iona, off the coast of present-day Scotland.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Anglo-Saxons

questions.q: Which saint became the patron saint of Ireland after preaching there?
questions.explain: St Patrick was a missionary in Ireland and is its patron saint.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Anglo-Saxons

questions.q: From which countries did the Vikings come?
questions.explain: The Vikings came from Denmark and Norway, first raiding Britain in AD 789.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Vikings

questions.q: In what year did the Vikings first visit Britain to raid coastal towns?
questions.explain: The Vikings first came to Britain in AD 789.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Vikings

questions.q: Which Anglo-Saxon king defeated the Vikings?
questions.explain: The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms united under King Alfred the Great, who defeated the Vikings.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Vikings

questions.q: What was the area of England settled by the Vikings called?
questions.explain: Many Vikings settled in the east and north of England, an area known as the Danelaw.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Vikings

questions.q: Which Danish king ruled England after the Anglo-Saxon kings?
questions.explain: Cnut, a Danish king, ruled England for a time before the Anglo-Saxon line returned.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Vikings

questions.q: Who is traditionally regarded as uniting the Scots and Picts into one kingdom?
questions.explain: Kenneth MacAlpin united the peoples of the north into a kingdom that became known as Scotland.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Vikings

questions.q: Which battle in 1066 brought William, Duke of Normandy, to the English throne?
questions.explain: William defeated the English king Harold at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Norman Conquest

questions.q: Which English king was killed at the Battle of Hastings?
questions.explain: King Harold was killed at Hastings and William of Normandy became king.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Norman Conquest

questions.q: What famous embroidery tells the story of the Norman Conquest?
questions.explain: The Bayeux Tapestry, now in France, shows the events of the Norman invasion.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Norman Conquest

questions.q: What was the Domesday Book?
options: A book of prayers written by monks
A record of towns, villages, landowners and animals in England after the Norman Conquest
A list of laws agreed by King John
questions.explain: William the Conqueror ordered a survey of England, recorded in the Domesday Book.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Norman Conquest

questions.q: Which statement about the Norman Conquest is correct?
options: The Normans conquered all of Scotland in 1066
The Normans conquered England but did not conquer Scotland
The Normans were defeated at Hastings
questions.explain: The Normans took England and some of Wales, but Scotland was not conquered.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Norman Conquest

questions.q: What language did the Norman kings and their followers speak?
questions.explain: After 1066 the ruling class spoke Norman French, which mixed with Anglo-Saxon to shape English.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Norman Conquest

questions.q: Which king annexed Wales to the Crown of England in 1284?
questions.explain: Edward I annexed Wales through the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Middle Ages

questions.q: Which law of 1284 annexed Wales to the English Crown?
questions.explain: The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 brought Wales under the English Crown.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Middle Ages

questions.q: Which castles did Edward I build to keep control of Wales?
questions.explain: Huge castles such as Conwy and Caernarvon were built to maintain power in Wales.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Middle Ages

questions.q: In which battle in 1314 did Robert the Bruce defeat the English?
questions.explain: Robert the Bruce's victory at Bannockburn meant Scotland remained unconquered by the English.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Middle Ages

questions.q: Who led the Scots to victory at the Battle of Bannockburn?
questions.explain: Robert the Bruce defeated the English at Bannockburn in 1314.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Middle Ages

questions.q: What was the name of the area around Dublin ruled by the English in the Middle Ages?
questions.explain: By 1200 the English controlled an area around Dublin known as the Pale.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Middle Ages

questions.q: What were the Crusades?
options: Civil wars between the houses of York and Lancaster
Wars in which European Christians fought for control of the Holy Land
questions.explain: Knights from England took part in the Crusades to win control of the Holy Land.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Middle Ages

questions.q: How long did the Hundred Years War with France actually last?
questions.explain: Despite its name, the Hundred Years War lasted 116 years.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch3 A long and illustrious history: The Middle Ages

questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The media and government

questions.q: What must UK broadcasters ensure when covering political parties?
options: Balanced coverage of the different parties
Only coverage of the two largest parties
questions.explain: By law, radio and TV coverage of political parties must be balanced.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The media and government

questions.q: What is the minimum age for voting in UK Parliament general elections?
questions.explain: The voting age for general elections was lowered from 21 to 18 in 1969.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Who can vote

questions.q: In what year was the voting age reduced to 18?
questions.explain: In 1969 the voting age for men and women was reduced to 18.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Who can vote

questions.q: Who can vote in UK general elections?
options: UK citizens, and Irish and eligible Commonwealth citizens resident in the UK, aged 18 or over
Only people born in the UK
Anyone living in the UK for one year, regardless of nationality
questions.explain: UK citizens, and Irish and eligible Commonwealth citizens resident in the UK, can vote in UK general elections from age 18. (Rules for devolved and local elections differ: in Scotland and Wales the voting age is 16.)
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Who can vote

questions.q: What must you do before you can vote?
options: Register to vote (be on the electoral register)
questions.explain: You must be on the electoral register, held by your local authority.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Who can vote

questions.q: Which statement about voting in UK elections is correct?
options: Voting is compulsory and you are fined if you don't vote
You must tell your employer how you voted
Votes are counted by the Prime Minister
questions.explain: Votes are cast in secret and no one can be forced to reveal their vote.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Who can vote

questions.q: If you cannot go to a polling station on election day, how else might you vote?
questions.explain: You can register for a postal vote.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Who can vote

questions.q: Who can stand for election as an MP?
options: Only members of the House of Lords
UK, Irish or eligible Commonwealth citizens aged 18 or over, with some exceptions
questions.explain: Some people, such as members of the armed forces and civil servants, cannot stand.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Standing for office

questions.q: How can you meet your MP to discuss an issue?
questions.explain: Many MPs hold regular surgeries where constituents can meet them.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Contacting elected members

questions.q: Can members of the public watch debates in the House of Commons?
options: Yes, from the public galleries, free of charge
questions.explain: The public can watch debates in Parliament for free.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Visiting Parliament

questions.q: What is the Commonwealth?
options: A trade union of European countries
A military alliance led by the USA
A voluntary association of countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire
questions.explain: Commonwealth members support democracy, the rule of law and human rights; membership is voluntary.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The UK and international institutions

questions.q: The UK is a permanent member of which body?
questions.explain: The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The UK and international institutions

questions.q: What is NATO?
options: A group of European and North American countries that have agreed to help each other if attacked
questions.explain: The UK is a member of NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization).
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The UK and international institutions

questions.q: Which organisation, separate from the EU, created the European Convention on Human Rights?
questions.explain: The UK is a member of the Council of Europe, which drew up the ECHR.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The UK and international institutions

questions.q: Which UK law incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law?
options: The Representation of the People Act 1969
questions.explain: The Human Rights Act 1998 made ECHR rights enforceable in UK courts.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The UK and international institutions

questions.q: Which of these is a right protected by the European Convention on Human Rights?
options: The right to a free car
The right to avoid all taxes
The right to choose your own judge
Freedom of thought, conscience and religion
questions.explain: ECHR rights include the right to life, freedom from torture, the right to a fair trial and freedom of expression.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The UK and international institutions

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a criminal offence?
questions.explain: Criminal law deals with crimes; the others are civil matters.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The law

questions.q: Which of these is an example of civil law?
options: A dispute between a landlord and a tenant
questions.explain: Civil law settles disputes between individuals or groups, such as housing, employment or debt.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The law

questions.q: Which of these is a criminal offence?
options: Refusing a refund in a shop
Selling tobacco products to anyone under 18
questions.explain: Selling tobacco to under-18s is a crime.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The law

questions.q: Which of these actions is against the criminal law?
questions.explain: It is a crime to buy alcohol for a person under 18.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The law

questions.q: Where is smoking banned by law?
options: In almost all enclosed public places
questions.explain: Smoking is not allowed in nearly all enclosed public places.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The law

questions.q: Which of these is a civil matter rather than a criminal one?
options: A claim for compensation after an injury
questions.explain: Personal injury claims are dealt with under civil law.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The law

questions.q: Which of these is a duty of the police?
options: To protect life and property and prevent and detect crime
questions.explain: The police protect life and property, prevent disturbances and prevent and detect crime.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The police

questions.q: Which statement about the police is correct?
options: Police forces are independent of the government
The Prime Minister directs individual arrests
The police are part of the army
Each MP controls a local police force
questions.explain: The police are organised into separate forces headed by Chief Constables and are independent of government.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The police

questions.q: What are PCSOs?
options: Police community support officers who support police officers on the streets
questions.explain: PCSOs patrol the streets, help the public and support the police.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The police

questions.q: Who can you complain to about police misconduct in Northern Ireland?
options: The Speaker of the House of Commons
questions.explain: In Northern Ireland complaints go to the Police Ombudsman.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The police

questions.q: What should you do if you think someone is planning a terrorist attack?
options: Report it to the police, confidentially if you wish
questions.explain: Anyone who suspects terrorist activity should contact the police; reports can be made confidentially.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The police

questions.q: Which court deals with most minor criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
questions.explain: Almost all criminal cases start in a Magistrates' Court.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: Which statement about magistrates is correct?
options: They are usually unpaid and do not need legal qualifications
They are elected by the public
They work only in the Supreme Court
questions.explain: Magistrates (Justices of the Peace) are usually unpaid volunteers who receive training.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: In Scotland, which court deals with minor criminal offences?
options: The Justice of the Peace Court
questions.explain: Minor criminal offences in Scotland go to a Justice of the Peace Court.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: Which court deals with serious criminal offences in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
questions.explain: Serious offences are tried in the Crown Court before a judge and jury.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: How many people sit on a jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
questions.explain: A jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland has 12 members.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: How many people sit on a jury in Scotland?
questions.explain: Scottish juries have 15 members.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: In Scotland, where are the most serious criminal cases tried?
questions.explain: Serious cases in Scotland go to the High Court; most others are heard in Sheriff Courts.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which court deals with young people accused of crimes?
questions.explain: Youth courts hear cases involving 10- to 17-year-olds; the public are not allowed in and the young person's identity is protected.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: What system deals with children and young people who commit offences in Scotland?
questions.explain: Scotland uses Children's Hearings to deal with young offenders.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: Which courts deal with civil disputes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
questions.explain: County Courts deal with civil disputes such as debts, personal injury and family matters.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: What is the small claims procedure used for?
options: Settling claims for small amounts of money without a formal court hearing
questions.explain: In England and Wales it applies to claims under £10,000.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: In England and Wales, below what amount can a claim normally be dealt with by the small claims procedure?
questions.explain: The small claims limit in England and Wales is £10,000.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: The courts

questions.q: Where can you get free advice about your legal rights?
questions.explain: Citizens Advice gives free advice; solicitors also give advice, usually for a fee.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Legal advice

questions.q: What is meant by 'the rule of law'?
options: The monarch can ignore the law
Everyone, including those in power, must obey the law
Only citizens must obey the law
questions.explain: No one is above the law, including the government.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Fundamental principles

questions.q: Under the Equality Act 2010, which of these is a protected characteristic?
questions.explain: Protected characteristics include age, disability, sex, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sexual orientation, gender reassignment, and marriage or civil partnership.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Equal opportunities

questions.q: Which statement about discrimination at work is correct?
options: Employers may refuse to hire women
It is illegal to discriminate against someone because of their disability
Employers may pay people less because of their race
Discrimination is legal in small companies
questions.explain: Disability is a protected characteristic under equality law.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Equal opportunities

questions.q: Which body works to promote equality and human rights in England, Scotland and Wales?
options: The Equality and Human Rights Commission
questions.explain: The Equality and Human Rights Commission has responsibility for enforcing equality legislation.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Equal opportunities

questions.q: Which statement about domestic violence in the UK is correct?
options: It is legal if the couple are married
It is a private matter the police cannot deal with
Only physical violence by men is a crime
It is a serious crime, whether or not the people are married
questions.explain: Anyone who is violent towards their partner – man or woman, married or not – can be prosecuted.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Domestic violence

questions.q: What does UK law say about female genital mutilation (FGM)?
options: It is a crime, including arranging for it to be done abroad
It is legal if done by a doctor
It is legal if the family agrees
It is only illegal in Scotland
questions.explain: FGM is illegal in the UK, and it is a crime to take a girl abroad for it.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Female genital mutilation

questions.q: Which statement about marriage in the UK is correct?
options: Marriage must be entered into with the full and free consent of both people
Parents can choose a spouse without the person's consent
Forced marriage is legal if it takes place abroad
Only men need to consent to marriage
questions.explain: Forced marriage is against the law; courts can issue Forced Marriage Protection Orders.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Forced marriage

questions.q: How is income tax normally paid by employees?
options: In cash at the post office
It is deducted from wages automatically by the employer (PAYE)
It is not paid by employees
questions.explain: Pay As You Earn means tax is taken from wages by the employer.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Taxation

questions.q: Who must complete a Self Assessment tax return?
options: Self-employed people (and some others with untaxed income)
questions.explain: Self-employed people must pay their own tax through Self Assessment.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Taxation

questions.q: What are National Insurance contributions used to pay for?
options: State benefits and services such as the state pension and the NHS
questions.explain: National Insurance contributions help fund benefits, the state pension and the NHS.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Taxation

questions.q: What is a National Insurance number?
options: A unique personal account number that makes sure your contributions are recorded
questions.explain: Everyone needs a National Insurance number before starting work.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Taxation

questions.q: What is the minimum age to drive a car on public roads?
questions.explain: You must be at least 17 to drive a car or ride a motorcycle; 16 for a moped.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Driving

questions.q: Which of these must you have before driving a car on public roads?
questions.explain: It is illegal to drive without a licence or insurance.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Driving

questions.q: In Great Britain, vehicles older than how many years must pass an MOT test each year?
questions.explain: In Great Britain, cars over three years old need an annual MOT test (in Northern Ireland the first test is at four years).
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Driving

questions.q: Which statement about using a mobile phone while driving is correct?
options: It is legal at slow speeds
It is illegal to use a hand-held mobile phone while driving
It is legal if you hold it to your ear
questions.explain: Using a hand-held phone while driving is against the law.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Driving

questions.q: How are people chosen for jury service?
options: At random from the electoral register
questions.explain: Anyone on the electoral register may be selected for jury service and must serve unless excused.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Your role in the community

questions.q: Which of these is a way of helping your community?
questions.explain: Volunteering is a good way to support your community and gain experience.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Your role in the community

questions.q: Which of these is a way you can help the environment?
options: Driving short distances instead of walking
questions.explain: Recycling and using public transport, walking or cycling help the environment.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Your role in the community

questions.q: Which of these is a way of helping in schools?
options: Setting exam papers for the government
Choosing head teachers in other countries
Becoming a school governor (or a member of a school board in Scotland)
questions.explain: School governors help set the strategic direction of schools.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Your role in the community

questions.q: Which of these is a way of helping others in the community that can save lives?
questions.explain: Blood donation saves lives; you can register to give blood at a donor centre.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Your role in the community

questions.q: Which statement about litter is correct?
options: Dropping litter is legal in cities
Dropping litter is a crime and you can be fined
Only businesses can be fined for litter
Litter is only an offence on beaches
questions.explain: Littering is an offence that can lead to a fine.
questions.ref: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents (3rd ed.), Ch5 The UK government, the law and your role: Your role in the community
